issues.note: Read literally, the Panama Canal also lets ships sail between Europe and Asia (East Asia and the Pacific) without going around Africa; it is a recognised if longer alternative for some voyages. The stem states an effect, not the link the canal makes, so a pedant can defend a second answer (card rule 2, guide 3.2). Reword to name the link, for example 'Which canal joins the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea?', or keep the shortcut idea with both seas named. The key claim changes, so it needs fresh checks.

claimResults.note: The waterway runs from 31.256 N on the Mediterranean shore (GeoNames puts Port Said at 31.26531, 32.3019) to 29.974 N at the head of the Gulf of Suez, the Red Sea's northern arm (GeoNames: Suez at 29.97371, 32.52627). A sea link between those two seas is what spares a Europe to Asia voyage the trip round Africa: the dataset gives the geography, and that routing step is my own reasoning. Cold solve Suez Canal, high confidence.

evidence.restatement: The Panama Canal crosses the Isthmus of Panama between the Caribbean (Atlantic) and the Pacific; the Kiel Canal runs across Schleswig-Holstein from Brunsbüttel on the Elbe estuary to Kiel on the Baltic; the Corinth Canal cuts the Isthmus of Corinth between the Gulf of Corinth and the Saronic Gulf.

evidence.restatement: The Suez Canal is a sea-level cut with no locks: the Mediterranean and the Gulf of Suez stand at nearly the same mean level, so water flows freely along it. Napoleon's surveyors wrongly thought the Red Sea stood about 10 m higher, which would have meant locks; later levelling found the two seas nearly equal.

The 'because' is the usual account: near-equal sea levels let the canal run without locks, with the low, flat isthmus making a sea-level cut practical.

evidence.restatement: The Panama Canal lifts ships about 26 m through lock flights (Gatun on the Atlantic side, Pedro Miguel and Miraflores on the Pacific side, plus the newer Agua Clara and Cocolí locks) up to Gatun Lake and lowers them again on the far side.

issues.note: Rival test on Panama: a ship can sail west from Europe through the Panama Canal to East Asia without passing Africa, but that canal saves the voyage round South America and is not known as a Europe to Asia link. With 'without going around Africa' in the stem, only Suez fits. Not a second answer.

Explanation: 'Unlike the Panama Canal, it needs no locks, because the seas at its two ends lie at almost the same level' invites the reading that Panama has locks because its oceans stand at different levels. Panama's locks lift ships over high ground to Gatun Lake (about 26 m up); the two oceans' mean levels differ only slightly. Optional rewording for the editor, under the re-check rule: 'It needs no locks, because the seas at its two ends lie at almost the same level. The Panama Canal uses locks to lift ships over the hills between its oceans.'
